snippet.title: D-Day, Normandy 1944: The Espionage Plot That Changed WW2 | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
June 6, 1944: nearly 130,000 Allied soldiers land on the beaches of Normandy in the largest amphibious invasion in history. But long before the first troops reached France, a secret war of deception was already underway. This documentary reveals how British intelligence and a network of double agents helped mislead Adolf Hitler and the German High Command in the crucial weeks before D-Day. Through Operation Fortitude, MI5 operatives created fake armies, false radio traffic, and carefully controlled intelligence designed to convince the Nazis that the real invasion would come at Pas-de-Calais instead of Normandy.

Featuring legendary spies such as Juan Pujol Garcia, code-named “Garbo,” this documentary uncovers the extraordinary espionage campaign that helped change the course of World War II. From double agents and deception networks to secret operations that fooled Hitler himself, this is the untold story behind the success of D-Day.

Briell Decker is a former plural wife of Warren Jeffs, leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, or FLDS, a polygamist sect widely considered a cult.

Decker married Jeffs at 18 and spent eight years inside the group while it was being investigated by several law enforcement agencies. Decker explains how the FLDS manipulated its members, including through arranged marriages, financial control, isolation, and the use of religious authority to enforce obedience. She also describes her multiple escape attempts and the pressure the church used to keep members from leaving.

Warren Jeffs was arrested in 2006 and, in 2011, was sentenced to life in prison plus 20 years for sexually assaulting underage girls.

Decker now works with people leaving polygamist communities as founder of the Short Creek Dream Center. She appeared in the HBO Max/Discovery+ documentary "Prisoner of the Prophet."

If you are a survivor of sexual assault, you can call the National Sexual Assault Hotline (1-800-656-4673) or visit its website to receive confidential support.

snippet.description:
When two British businessmen lose $4.5 million in gems in a brazen New York hotel heist, detectives uncover a plot far more shocking than a simple robbery.

Dive into the true story of Darius Guppy and Benedict Marsh, two entrepreneurs with royal connections, whose apparent victimhood unravels into an audacious international fraud. This video breaks down the twists behind the 1990 Halloran House Hotel gem robbery, from the high-stakes world of jewel trading to the dark side of business ambition. Predicting the next war would be fought over ownership, the Americans launched a huge expedition to Antarctica, Operation Highjump, sending 13 ships, 33 planes and 5,000 men to stake their claim on the polar environment.

Once there, they established a temporary base, conducted aerial surveys, photographed and mapped huge stretches of coastline, and tested ships, aircraft and survival techniques in extreme cold, laying the groundwork for future operations in one of the most hostile places on Earth.

snippet.title: XPLOSION: Inside South Africa’s Underground Taxi Raves
snippet.description:
In 1980s South Africa during Apartheid, racist “influx control” laws made it almost impossible for black taxi drivers to earn a living. They upgraded their sedans to minibuses and worked illegally, providing vital transport for their communities. The end of Apartheid created a new problem, as the underground taxi network was replaced by a cutthroat system where corruption thrived and competition over routes turned brutally violent. Intimidation and targeted killings became commonplace.

Deaths in the “Taxi Wars” peaked in the late 90s, but the industry remains highly dangerous. Even now, most assassinations in South Africa are related to taxi violence. And while most drivers are armed with some kind of weapon, most are just men trying to feed their families.

For the young and the bored, the taxis sometimes perform a different function, providing a confined space with a dance floor the size of a phone box where they can listen to gqom at deafening volume and take umgwinyo: a synthetic drug, like ecstasy, that they use to summon the spirits of the dead.

The events, called Umqhumo (which translates as “explosion”), are held in secret locations where Durban’s humid jungle sprawl meets the Indian Ocean. Taxis line up beside one another in formation, each run by a different team that produces its own music for the night, with a dedicated MC and loyal followers. VICE rode along with Team Orange, hosted by producer Papa J and lead “party guy” Junior Mike.

snippet.title: Sensors On James Webb Camera
snippet.description:
The James Webb Telescope observes the universe in infrared light, allowing it to detect objects and phenomena invisible in visible wavelengths.

Its MIRI instrument (Mid-Infrared Instrument) is extremely sensitive, designed to measure faint thermal emissions from distant stars, galaxies, and planetary systems. To prevent the telescope’s own heat from interfering with these measurements, its cameras are maintained at –234°C.

This precise temperature control, combined with advanced detector technology, ensures that even the faintest infrared signals from billions of light-years away can be accurately captured, providing unprecedented insight into the formation and evolution of the cosmos.

snippet.title: The Secret Notes: Writing in Secret Under German Occupation - Full Documentary
snippet.description:
A plastic bag at a charity shop. Nine notebooks inside. And 2,000 pages of a secret diary written under German occupation — that no one had read in over a century. 📓 

Inside: nine notebooks. 2,000 handwritten pages. Newspaper clippings, drawings, photographs.
A diary written in secret — during the First World War — by a man living under German occupation in northern France.

Achille Bourgin was 33 years old. A postal worker. A father. Deemed unfit to fight due to tuberculosis.
But when the Germans occupied his city of Douai, he made a decision that would define his life: he would not comply. He went into hiding. And he began to write.

Every day. Sometimes under bombardment. A precise, intimate, unflinching account of what it meant to live — not on the front line — but trapped behind it. Hungry. Afraid. Cut off from the rest of France.
 
Forced into silence.
Bourgin refused that silence.

Through his pages, we hear the voices of an entire occupied population that history almost forgot — civilians caught between two armies, with no weapons, no news, and no way out.

His diary survived the war. It survived a century of obscurity.
Found by chance. Read for the first time.
This is his story.

If you enjoy uncovering hidden chapters of history, don’t forget to like 👍, subscribe 🔔, and share to support more documentaries like this!
